haiku-low.q1: Before. Startup loads all three keys before the server accepts traffic. The instance is marked ready only after all three load successfully.
haiku-low.q2: It retries, then exits non-zero and never becomes ready. Old pods keep serving, so the new instance gets no live traffic and the rollout halts.
haiku-low.q3: A timer re-reads each key every 5 minutes and swaps in a new version. On failure it keeps the last good value, logs a warning, and readiness is unchanged.
haiku-low.q4: Values live only in memory, in per-secret holders. They must never appear in logs, config files, environment variables, disk, or crash dumps.
haiku-low.q5: Only the orders-api-prod identity reads prod values. Only the security on-call role writes them. Engineers have no prod read access.
haiku-low.q6: Git history is not rewritten, so keys stay leaked. Old keys become harmless only when rotated at providers and then revoked after the rollout is confirmed.
haiku-low.q7: Each client receives the secret provider at construction and calls get() per request. The holder swaps whole records, and in-flight requests keep their snapshot.
haiku-low.q8: Each pod must log the new version ids for all three keys in the central log service. Security on-call checks manually, confirms no old pods remain, and records the result.
haiku-low.q9: Set store access, rotate keys at providers, copy new keys into the store, then switch the app to read the store and remove keys from the committed file in the same change.
haiku-low.q10: make run loads dev keys from orders-api/dev using the developer's own dev identity, held in memory. make run-offline uses stub clients and needs no key.
haiku-low.q11: It retries, then logs an error naming the missing secret and exits non-zero. The pod never becomes ready, and the two loaded keys are not used for readiness.

sonnet.q1: Keys are loaded first, before the server accepts traffic. Only after all three load does the process mark itself ready; readiness (/healthz) returns 200 only after startup loading succeeded.
sonnet.q2: It retries (first attempt plus 3 retries, 2 seconds apart), then logs an error and exits non-zero. The cluster restarts it with backoff; it never becomes ready, so the rollout halts and old pods keep serving. Live traffic is unaffected. On-call is paged and must fix the store or roll back.
sonnet.q3: A timer in the same process refreshes every 5 minutes (the only trigger): it fetches the current version and, if the version id is new, swaps the holder and logs the version change. If the read fails, it keeps the last good value and logs a warning (secret name, error type, last good version id, age). Readiness does not change; an alert fires if the value gets too old (threshold not yet set).
sonnet.q4: Held in memory only, in a holder per key (value, version id, fetch time). They must never appear in the image, config file, environment variables, logs, disk or crash dumps (core dumps disabled). Also never in tickets, chat or files.
sonnet.q5: Read: the pod identity orders-api-prod (read on orders-api/prod/*, with prod KMS decrypt). Engineers have no read access to prod values. Write: only the security on-call role, on orders-api/prod/*; this is the only write path. orders-api-prod has no write access.
sonnet.q6: The keys stay in git history and in every old image (pre-migration images embed them), and git history is not rewritten. The old values are made harmless by rotating all keys at the providers and, after the rollout, bake period and sign-off, revoking the old keys so they stop working. The keys are treated as permanently leaked.
sonnet.q7: Each client gets the secret provider when built and does not copy the key. On each request it calls get('payments'/'email'/'geocoding'), which returns the holder's current value as a snapshot (value with version id). The refresh swaps the whole holder record, so the next request reads the new value. In-flight requests finish with the key they started with.
sonnet.q8: Each pod logs the secret name and version id for all three keys at startup and on each change, and these lines go to the central log service. The security on-call queries it for each pod's lines and records the result in the migration record (manual unless automated). They also confirm that no old ReplicaSet pod remains, including draining ones, and that provider error rates are at baseline. Then a bake period and sign-off follow.
sonnet.q9: 1) Confirm provider capabilities and inventory. 2) Prepare store access and KMS. 3) Create dev/staging secrets with sandbox keys. 4) Rotate keys at providers, keeping the old keys valid. 5) Write the new keys to the prod store, after a provider read-only check. 6) Merge the code and config change that removes keys from the committed file (plus the CI guard), build the image and check it in staging. 7) Roll out to prod, which switches the app to read from the store. Then confirm, bake, pass the revocation gate, and revoke old keys. Cleanup is last.
sonnet.q10: From the dev secrets orders-api/dev/* in the store (sandbox keys), using the developer's own dev identity, which has no prod access. If there is no dev access or the store is down, make run-offline uses stub clients with no keys.
sonnet.q11: It treats that the same as the store being unreachable. It retries (first attempt plus 3 retries, 2 seconds apart). If it still fails, it logs an error naming the missing secret and the store error, exits non-zero, and never becomes ready. The cluster restarts it with backoff.
sonnet.q12: NOT STATED. Rotation cadence is an undecided open question; the plan picks no schedule.
